CF-VEG-LRT.title: Tree cover of Little Round Top
CF-VEG-LRT.why: Two web articles disagree (PDF B.10.3 and T2-076): "unwooded but steep and rocky" against "bare west slope with a lightly wooded summit and east and south slopes". The NPS Cultural Landscape Report of 2012 settles part of it: the east-slope tracts were wooded, the Hanaway tract on the west slope was cleared of most trees before 1863, and a tree line at the summit divided them (VC-NPS-026..028). Two more National Park Service statements agree on the west slope: a report of about 1940 says it had been cut clear a year before the battle (VC-NPSC-VISTA-CUTTING-p010-01, no source given for the date) and that the Brady photographs taken after the battle show it nearly devoid of trees (VC-NPSC-VISTA-CUTTING-p011-01c); the same report reads a considerable growth of pine and oak scattered on the west slope on the Warren map of 1868-69, five years later (VC-NPSC-VISTA-CUTTING-p011-01b): growth after the battle, not the state of 1863.

nps_clr.label: NPS CLR 2012: west slope cleared, summit tree line, east slope wooded

wiki_unwooded.label: Battlefield article: the whole hill unwooded, steep and rocky

wiki_light_summit.label: Little Round Top article: bare west face, lightly wooded summit, east and south slopes

CF-VEG-RAIN.title: Wheat and oats after the rain of 3-4 July
CF-VEG-RAIN.why: The plan says the trample mask is overwritten by rain flattening on 4 July. The only source read on rain damage to the crop is the Gettysburg Compiler of 27 July 1863: the damage of the late heavy rains will in no case exceed five per cent of the crop (VC-LIB-015, where the cut wheat is also said to have been garnered). Nothing read measures the rain of 4 July on standing crops.

gaps.title: Which crop each field cell held
gaps.what: No source read assigns a crop to the fields of the open ground except the Wheatfield and the few fields in claims that can be placed (role exact or nearest). Every other cell takes its crop from the district mix by a seeded draw.
gaps.why: The 1860 census schedules and the 1868 damage-claim files are not read; the NPS inventories give field numbers whose outlines are in GIS layers the repository does not hold.

gaps.title: Field boundaries inside the open ground
gaps.what: The cut lines that divide a block of open ground into field cells are straight cuts across the long axis of each piece, placed by a seed, not a map. Roads, lanes, the railway and the 30 confirmed fence lines bound the blocks; wood, orchard and marsh edges are the Warren outlines.
gaps.why: Fence lines other than the 30 confirmed ones are not mapped for 1863 (362 of 392 candidates are modern reconstructions or unchecked).

gaps.title: Ripeness and cut date of each grain field
gaps.what: Wheat stood nearly ripe on 2 July (documented) and was being cut in the last two weeks of July (documented); the date each field was cut, and rye, barley and oats, are ranged.
gaps.why: No farmer's diary, harvest notice or photograph of 5-14 July with a dated field was found. The 1863 Compiler and Adams Sentinel (June to August) were searched by keyword, not read page by page; that reading is owed.

gaps.title: Grass height and mowing dates of the hay meadows
gaps.what: Meadows were grassy on the morning of 2 July; new hay existed by 10 July in Maryland; the mowing date of each meadow is a seeded draw.
gaps.why: No source gives a grass height.

gaps.title: Fruit state of the orchards
gaps.what: Cherries were ripe on 2 and 5 July (documented); apples, peaches, pears and plums have no sourced state; the viewer is told so.
gaps.why: Same as EG-0020: no sourced fruit-state account.

gaps.title: Species and age of woodlot and orchard trees
gaps.what: The family (oak-hickory) is sourced for two woodlots; chestnut and black locust are shown present by the fence timber; every share, every height and the age of orchards other than the named young orchards are ranges.
gaps.why: The NPS Historic Vegetation Study and the 1860 census are not in the library (register EG-0139, EG-0143); the plan lists "no sourced species list for Culp's Hill or Big Round Top".

gaps.title: Understory of the ridge forests
gaps.what: Farm woodlots had an open understory (documented). Kershaw (2 July) gives thick undergrowth on the stony hill behind the Rose house and a scrubby interval of about 100 yards beyond it (documented, placed by a rule); Greene and Jones call Culp's Hill rocky, wooded and heavily timbered, with no word on the undergrowth. The understory of the rest of Culp's Hill, Big Round Top and Houck's Ridge is not described.
gaps.why: The Official Records reports were searched for timber, forest, undergrowth, scrub and thicket; a report that search did not find was not read through.

gaps.title: Individual tree positions
gaps.what: Every tree is placed by a seeded scatter inside its polygon, in rows for orchards; only the witness trees named in claims (the large oak at the Trostle lane, the tree at the Codori lane) have a documented place and none of them is placed to better than the polygon.

gaps.title: Little Round Top tree cover
gaps.what: Carried as three selectable readings; the NPS Cultural Landscape Report supports the first, and a second National Park Service report (about 1940) agrees on the west slope: cut clear a year before the battle (no source given for the date), nearly bare in the Brady photographs taken after it, with the pine and oak the Warren map shows there five years later read as later growth.
gaps.why: Two web articles conflict; the reports settle the west slope and the east slope, not every tree. The Brady photographs themselves were not read (G13).

gaps.title: Vegetation on 19 November 1863
gaps.what: Leaf-off is documented by one remark; the field stages are drawn per field from the calendar.
gaps.why: The plan lists "No Nov 19 vegetation source".

gaps.title: Extent and degree of trampling and tree damage
gaps.what: That fields were trampled (2 July, Haskell; the Wheatfield in the OR reports) and that trees were stripped or splintered (Culp's Hill, Herbst Woods, the orchards) is documented; the share of each field or stand affected is ranged and follows the troops the theatre draws.
gaps.why: No survey of the damage by field exists in the sources read; the 1868 damage claims give acreages destroyed per farm, not where.

gaps.title: Damage-claim acreages of farms not yet read
gaps.what: Eight farms' crop acreages are read (McPherson, Wills, Harman, Forney, Slyder, Josiah Benner, Abraham Spangler, Trostle; the Bushman claim names crops without acreage); the Rose, Sherfy, Codori, Weikert, Wentz, Bliss, Rogers, McClean and other claims are not.
gaps.why: The claim files are not in the library; the NPS reports quote some of them. Found in the saved reports and not used: the Biesecker claim (12 acres of wheat, 3.5 of corn, 10 of oats) and the Bollinger claim (a tenant's share of the crop) in the Eisenhower National Historic Site study, and the McClean claim, whose table has ditto marks; their print is garbled in the saved text, so no acreage is taken from them until the pages are read from the page images.

gaps.title: Photographs of 5-14 July for stubble and trample state
gaps.what: No photograph is used for any vegetation state here. A National Park Service report says the Brady photographs of the post-battle period show the west slope of Little Round Top nearly devoid of trees, and cites photographs for the open character of Devil's Den; the photographs themselves were not read.
gaps.why: The photo-match catalogue exists (109 records); a field-by-field reading of stubble and trample is owed.

gaps.title: Gardens, potato patches, flax, buckwheat, hedgerows
gaps.what: Named in claims as present on the farms (hedgerows: grown mostly of themselves along fence lines and on rocky ground, of mixed trees, shrubs and briars, in the report's general account); none has a place, so none is drawn.

gaps.title: Modern trees in the ground photograph
gaps.what: The terrain is draped with a 2022 aerial photograph that shows modern woods and hedgerows; the field decals cover them where a field cell is drawn, but a modern tree that stands on a road verge, a fence line or in the town stays in the picture.
gaps.why: The prototype terrain texture is fixed.

gaps.title: Chestnut and the later changes to the woods
gaps.what: American chestnut is drawn as a living tree of the woodlots in ranged shares (a fifth or less of the trees: the NPS says the fences of the period were mostly chestnut and black locust, and that the hickory, chestnut and oak stands of Little Round Top had been harvested several times); the blight that later removed it, which the plan dates to about 1904, is not in any text read, so no blight, no dead chestnut and no modern species list is used, and nothing is drawn of the changes after 1863 that the park reports (replanting, regrowth, clearing: ground claims).
gaps.why: The date of the blight is general knowledge, not a retrieved non-lead source (PDF B.10.3 says "verify"); the modern lists the park publishes are of the woods as they are now and are not read into 1863.

claims.says: The Trostle farm petition of 1868: 27 acres of wheat, 9 of corn, 8 of oats, 4 of barley, 1 of flax, 1 of potatoes, 32 of grass and 20 tons of hay in the barn were destroyed.
claims.quote: 27 acres wheat destroyed, worth $600.00 9 acres Corn 360.00 8 acres Oats 80.00 4 acres Barley 50.00 1 acre Flax 15.00 1 acre Potatoes 50.00 32 acres Grass 650.00 20 tons of Hay out of the barn
claims.note: Printed in the National Park Service Civil War Series, The Battle of Gettysburg, section 20 (a petition of Catherine Trostle under the Pennsylvania act of 9 April 1868). The acreage is what she claimed destroyed.

claims.says: The Trostle farm lay between the two armies and was in part fought over several times; the petition says the crops and fences were totally destroyed.
claims.quote: the farm being between the two armies, in part was fought over several times
claims.note: A claimant's statement; 'totally destroyed' is hers. Used as documentation that the fields near the Trostle farm were trampled on 2 July, not for the degree.

claims.says: The Trostle claim states the farm, near Round Top, was fought over two days and the crops and fences totally destroyed.
claims.quote: that their farm was near Round Top, and was fought over two days, and the crops and fences were totally destroyed
